claim: Germfree mice develop worsened clinical disease following JHMV infection compared to SPF mice, with peak disease at day 13 maintained through 21 days post-infection.
source: As is typical in this model, infected SPF mice reach peak clinical disease by day 10–11 post-infection (p.i.) followed by a reduction of symptoms that plateaus around day 15–16 p.i. In contrast, GF mice developed worsened clinical disease that peaks at day 13 and is maintained through 21 days p.i. (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by clinical scoring data presented in Figure 1A showing disease progression over time, and the text explicitly describes the differences in disease kinetics between SPF and GF mice.

claim: Germfree mice have impaired control of JHMV viral replication at 14 days post-infection and virus is still present at 21 days post-infection.
source: While GF mice had slightly lower titers of virus within the brain at 7 days p.i., control of viral replication was impaired at 14-days p.i. and virus was still present in GF mice at 21 days p.i., a time point where SPF animals have almost undetectable levels of infectious viral particles (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by viral titer measurements from brain tissue at multiple time points shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Germfree mice display significantly more demyelination in the spinal cord compared to SPF animals following JHMV infection.
source: Importantly, GF mice displayed enhanced neurologic damage, as there was significantly more demyelination in the spinal cord when compared to SPF animals (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological analysis and quantification of demyelination shown in Figures 1C and 1D.

claim: Fewer total cells are recovered from the CNS of germfree mice during peak viral infection at day 7 post-infection.
source: Fewer total cells were recovered from the CNS of GF mice during peak viral infection (day 7) (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data quantifying total brain cells shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Germfree mice have a reduced frequency of total CNS-infiltrating CD4+ and CD8+ T cells at day 7 post-infection.
source: Moreover, there was a reduced frequency of total CNS-infiltrating CD4+ and CD8+ T cells (Figure 1F,G)
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data showing frequencies of CD4+ and CD8+ T cells in Figures 1F and 1G.

claim: Germfree mice have fewer viral-specific CD4+ and CD8+ T cells in the CNS at day 7 post-infection.
source: and fewer viral-specific CD4+ and CD8+ T cells in GF mice at day 7 p.i. (Figure 1H,I).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data measuring virus-specific T cells through IFN-γ production shown in Figures 1H and 1I.

claim: At day 21 post-infection, germfree mice show reductions only in total CD8+ and viral-specific CD8+ T cells compared to SPF mice.
source: These differences are diminished at a chronic timepoint (day 21), as reductions in only total CD8+ and viral-specific CD8+ T cells are observed (Figure 1G–I).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data at day 21 shown in Figures 1G-I.

claim: Germfree mice have increased CNS infiltrating Tregs during the acute phase of infection at day 7 post-infection.
source: GF mice have increased CNS infiltrating Tregs during the acute phase of infection (7 p.i)
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data measuring FoxP3+ CD4+ T cells referenced in the text.

claim: Germfree mice have a paucity of Tregs in the CNS during the chronic demyelinating phase of disease.
source: however, there is a paucity of Tregs in infected GF mice during the chronic demyelinating phase of disease (Figure 1J).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data showing Treg frequencies at chronic timepoints in Figure 1J.

claim: CD4 and CD8 T cells control viral replication in the JHMV model through secretion of anti-viral cytokines and cytolytic activity.
source: Virus-specific T cells control viral replication through secretion of anti-viral cytokines and cytolytic activity.
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge about the JHMV model without specific data in this manuscript.

claim: Tregs play a critical role in controlling neuroinflammation in response to JHMV infection.
source: Inflammation is controlled by the presence of CD4+, FoxP3+ T regulatory (Tregs) cells and previous reports have shown a critical role for these cells in controlling neuroinflammation in response to JHMV infection (Anghelina et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work by Anghelina et al., 2009.

claim: Lifelong antibiotic-treated mice develop worsened chronic disease following JHMV infection compared to SPF mice.
source: Similar to what was observed in GF mice, lifelong antibiotic-treated infected animals developed worsened chronic disease when compared to animals with an intact microbiota (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: The claim is supported by clinical scoring data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Lifelong antibiotic-treated mice are unable to control JHMV viral replication.
source: and were unable to control viral replication (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by viral titer data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: CD4+ T cells from germfree mice are not intrinsically deficient in their ability to respond to JHMV or traffic to the CNS.
source: Importantly, there were no differences observed in the recruitment of either CD4+ or CD8+ T cells derived from either GF or SPF mice to the CNS of JHMV-infected Rag1-/- mice, nor were there differences in CNS viral burden (Figure 2B–G). Collectively, these data show that neither CD4+ or CD8+ T cells from GF mice are intrinsically deficient in their ability to respond to JHMV or traffic to the CNS.
evidence: The claim is supported by adoptive transfer experiments showing no differences in T cell recruitment or viral control in Figures 2B-G.

claim: CD8+ T cells from germfree mice are not intrinsically deficient in their ability to respond to JHMV or traffic to the CNS.
source: Importantly, there were no differences observed in the recruitment of either CD4+ or CD8+ T cells derived from either GF or SPF mice to the CNS of JHMV-infected Rag1-/- mice, nor were there differences in CNS viral burden (Figure 2B–G). Collectively, these data show that neither CD4+ or CD8+ T cells from GF mice are intrinsically deficient in their ability to respond to JHMV or traffic to the CNS.
evidence: The claim is supported by adoptive transfer experiments showing no differences in T cell recruitment or viral control in Figures 2B-G.

claim: The microbiota exerts effects on alternate cell types (not T cells) to protect from JHMV infection within the CNS.
source: Thus, these data suggest that the microbiota exerts effects on alternate cell types to protect from viral infection within the CNS.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the adoptive transfer experiments showing T cells are not intrinsically defective.

claim: Germfree mice have a lower frequency of MHC class II+ microglia under homeostatic conditions.
source: We identified a lower frequency of MHC class II + microglia in uninfected GF mice (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data in Figures 3A and 3B.

claim: Antibiotic treatment decreases both the percentage of total microglia and the number of MHC expressing microglia in uninfected animals.
source: Disruption to the microbiota with antibiotics decreases both the percentage of total microglia and the number of MHC expressing microglia in uninfected animals (Figure 3C–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data in Figures 3C-F.

claim: CD86 and CD40 expression is significantly reduced on microglia from uninfected germfree mice.
source: Presentation of antigens requires co-stimulatory molecules such as CD86 and CD40 which are significantly reduced in expression on microglia from uninfected GF mice (Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1H.

claim: Expression of Ciita mRNA transcripts is significantly reduced in microglia isolated from germfree or antibiotic-treated mice compared to SPF mice.
source: Expression of Ciita mRNA transcripts is significantly reduced in microglia isolated from GF or antibiotic-treated mice compared to SPF mice, further corroborating a reduction in the antigen presentation machinery in the absence of microbes (Figure 3H,I) (Butovsky et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data in Figures 3H and 3I.

claim: Microglia from antibiotic-treated mice have reduced ability to induce CD8+ T cell proliferation when presenting the immunodominant JHMV peptide S510–518.
source: Corroborating the reduced antigen presentation markers on microglia from antibiotic-treated mice, the ability of these microglia to induce T cell proliferation was reduced when presenting the immunodominant JHMV peptide S510–518 (Figure 3J).
evidence: The claim is supported by T cell proliferation assay data in Figure 3J.

claim: Administration of PLX-3397 one week prior to JHMV infection results in a marked reduction in microglia in both number and percentage at days 7 and 14 post-infection.
source: Administration of PLX-3397 1 week prior to JHMV infection of SPF mice resulted in a marked reduction in microglia (CD45lo, CD11b+, F4/80+ cells as determined by flow cytometric staining) in both number and percentage at days 7 and 14 p.i. (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data in Figures 4A and 4B.

claim: PLX-3397 treatment does not reduce splenic or CNS-infiltrating macrophage populations in JHMV-infected mice.
source: Similar to this study, we did not observe a reduction in either splenic (CD45+, CD11b+) or CNS-infiltrating macrophage (CD45hi, CD11b+) populations (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: Microglia depletion leads to enhanced mortality in JHMV-infected mice.
source: We observed enhanced mortality in JHMV-infected mice following microglia reduction that correlated with an impaired ability to control viral replication within the CNS (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by survival curve data in Figure 4C.

claim: Microglia depletion leads to impaired ability to control JHMV viral replication within the CNS.
source: We observed enhanced mortality in JHMV-infected mice following microglia reduction that correlated with an impaired ability to control viral replication within the CNS (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by viral titer data in Figure 4D.

claim: Microglia depletion leads to increased demyelination compared to control mice.
source: Most importantly, microglia depletion leads to increased demyelination compared to control mice (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological analysis and quantification in Figures 4E and 4F.

claim: Both CD4+ and CD8+ T cell responses are deficient in the absence of microglia during JHMV infection.
source: Similar to what we observe in GF mice, both CD4+ and CD8+ T cell responses are deficient in the absence of microglia and IFN-γ production from these cells is impaired (Figure 4G–l and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D; Figure 4—figure supplement 1E; Figure 4—figure supplement 1F; Figure 4—figure supplement 1G; Figure 4—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data in Figures 4G-I and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D-H.

claim: LPS and Pam3CysK4 significantly upregulate both the frequency of MHCII expressing BV2 cells and the total amount of MHCI per cell.
source: LPS (and to a lesser extent, the TLR1/2 heterodimer ligand Pam3CysK4) significantly upregulated both the frequency of MHCII expressing cells and the total amount of MHCI per cell (Figure 5A,B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data from BV2 cell line experiments in Figures 5A, 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Feeding germfree mice bacterial cell wall components (LPS and/or Pam3CysK4) results in reduced paralysis following JHMV infection.
source: Feeding GF mice bacterial cell wall components resulted in reduced paralysis and lower viral titers at day 9 p.i. (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by clinical scoring data in Figure 5C.

claim: Feeding germfree mice bacterial cell wall components (LPS and/or Pam3CysK4) results in lower viral titers at day 9 post-infection.
source: Feeding GF mice bacterial cell wall components resulted in reduced paralysis and lower viral titers at day 9 p.i. (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by viral titer data in Figure 5D.

claim: Feeding germfree mice LPS alone leads to increases in cell number in the CNS of JHMV-infected mice.
source: Feeding GF animals LPS alone, led to similar increases in cell number in the CNS of infected mice (Figure 5E)
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 5E.

claim: Feeding germfree mice LPS alone leads to more MHCII expressing microglia during JHMV infection.
source: Feeding GF animals LPS alone, led to similar increases in cell number in the CNS of infected mice (Figure 5E), more MHCII expressing microglia and increased CD4 T cell trafficking to the CNS during infection (Figure 5F,G).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 5F.

claim: Feeding germfree mice LPS alone leads to increased CD4 T cell trafficking to the CNS during JHMV infection.
source: Feeding GF animals LPS alone, led to similar increases in cell number in the CNS of infected mice (Figure 5E), more MHCII expressing microglia and increased CD4 T cell trafficking to the CNS during infection (Figure 5F,G).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 5G.

claim: TLR4-/- mice develop significantly worsened disease symptoms following JHMV infection compared to WT mice.
source: TLR4-/- mice had significantly worsened disease symptoms that were similar to GF mice (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by clinical scoring data in Figure 6A.

claim: TLR4-/- animals have significantly increased demyelination following JHMV infection.
source: Importantly, TLR4-/- animals had significantly increased demyelination, indicating that TLR4 signals are important for protection from neurologic damage (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological analysis and quantification in Figures 6B and 6C.

claim: Microglia from TLR4-/- animals express lower levels of MHCII under homeostatic conditions prior to infection.
source: Consistent with this, microglia, but not macrophages, from TLR4-/- animals express lower levels of MHCII under homeostatic conditions, prior to infection (Figure 6D,E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data in Figures 6D and 6E.

claim: TLR4-/- mice have lower total numbers of MHCII expressing microglia during JHMV infection compared to WT mice.
source: and lower total numbers of MHCII expressing microglia (and total microglia) during JHMV infection when compared to WT mice (Figure 6F and G).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data in Figures 6F and 6G.

claim: JHMV is unable to directly activate TLR4.
source: JHMV is unable to directly activate TLR4 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C), further arguing that microbiota-based signals function to prime microglia against CNS infection.
evidence: The claim is supported by HEK-Blue TLR4 detection assay data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: TLR2-/- animals have no difference in mortality or clinical presentation of disease following JHMV infection compared to WT mice.
source: Compared to WT mice, TLR2-/- animals had no difference in mortality (not shown) or clinical presentation of disease (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by clinical scoring data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: WT animals receiving TLR4-/- bone marrow develop disease similar to WT animals following JHMV infection.
source: Moreover, animals receiving either WT or TLR4-/- bone marrow, where most of the systemic hematopoietic system is replaced by TLR4 deficient cells, still develop disease similar to WT animals (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by clinical scoring data from bone marrow chimera experiments in Figure 7A.

claim: Nestin is not expressed in microglia.
source: To verify that Nestin is not expressed in microglia, we crossed the nestin-Cre driver to a Rosa-lox-stop-lox-eYFP animal, allowing us to fate map nestin (and thus YFP) expressing cells. While we could readily detect YFP expression within the CNS, we were unable to detect YFP+ cells in the microglia fraction (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A), further corroborating that nestin-Cre will not drive recombination in microglia.
evidence: The claim is supported by fate mapping experiments shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Infection of nestin-Cre; TLR4-fl/fl animals does not demonstrate a difference in clinical disease compared to WT animals following JHMV infection.
source: While infection of CNSΔTLR4 animals did not demonstrate a difference in clinical disease compared to WT animals (Figure 7B)
evidence: The claim is supported by clinical scoring data in Figure 7B.

claim: Disruption of TLR4 specifically within microglia leads to worsened paralysis following JHMV infection.
source: disruption of TLR4 specifically within microglia, lead to worsened paralysis (Figure 7C).
evidence: The claim is supported by clinical scoring data from CX3CR1CreER; TLR4-fl/fl mice in Figure 7C.

claim: Gut microbial signals can directly influence microglia function to prevent viral-induced neurologic diseases.
source: Collectively, these data demonstrate that gut microbial signals can directly influence microglia function to prevent viral-induced neurologic diseases.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the collective experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: JHMV infection results in an acute encephalomyelitis characterized by viral replication in astrocytes, microglia, and oligodendrocytes.
source: JHMV infection results in an acute encephalomyelitis characterized by viral replication in astrocytes, microglia, and oligodendrocytes (Bergmann et al., 2006) (Greenberg et al., 2014) (Blanc et al., 2014; Carbajal et al., 2010; Marro et al., 2016; Schrauf et al., 2008; Stiles et al., 2006; Chen et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Sterile immunity is not achieved following JHMV infection and virus persists within white matter tracts in surviving mice.
source: Sterile immunity is not achieved and virus persists within white matter tracts in surviving mice that subsequently develop an immune-mediated demyelinating disease (Bender and Weiss, 2010; Bergmann et al., 2006; Cheng et al., 2018; Lane and Hosking, 2010; Libbey et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Microglia are resident tissue phagocytes of the CNS that function in host defense and tissue homeostasis.
source: Microglia are resident tissue phagocytes of the CNS that function in host defense and tissue homeostasis.
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge about microglia.

claim: Microglia are impacted by the gut microbiota despite their location within the CNS.
source: Recent studies have shown that despite their location within the CNS, microglia are impacted by the gut microbiota (Erny et al., 2015; Matcovitch-Natan et al., 2016; Sampson et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Resident commensal species can instruct the development of regulatory and inflammatory immune cell subsets that aid to limit viral replication at mucosal sites.
source: Several studies have shown that resident commensal species can instruct the development of regulatory and inflammatory immune cell subsets that aid to limit viral replication at mucosal sites (Abt et al., 2012; Robinson and Pfeiffer, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The microbiota can enhance the infectivity of some viruses.
source: However, while the microbiota inhibits infection by some viruses, it can also enhance the infectivity of other viruses (Robinson and Pfeiffer, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Microglia isolated from germfree mice have an immature phenotype based on gene expression and morphological analysis.
source: Commensal microbes are necessary for proper microglia maturation, with gene expression and morphological analysis suggesting that microglia isolated from GF mice have an immature phenotype (Erny et al., 2015; Matcovitch-Natan et al., 2016; Sampson et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Microglia activate antigen-specific T cell responses through presentation of antigens via MHC molecules.
source: One role for microglia is to activate antigen-specific T cell responses through presentation of antigens via MHC molecules (Mack et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: CIITA is a transcription factor that is critical to the expression of MHCII.
source: CIITA is a transcription factor that is critical to the expression of MHCII expression (Mach et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: A reduction in microglia leads to a defect in control of JHMV replication within the CNS.
source: Indeed, recent studies have demonstrated that a reduction in microglia leads to a defect in control of JHMV replication within the CNS (Wheeler et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Short chain fatty acids are able to influence the morphology and transcriptome of microglia.
source: Previous reports have identified that short chain fatty acids (SCFAs) are able to influence the morphology and transcriptome of microglia (Erny et al., 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The BV2 cell line is an effective alternative model system for primary microglia cultures to study various cell biology aspects.
source: The BV2 cell line was originally developed by infecting primary microglial cell cultures with a -raf/v-myc oncogene carrying retrovirus (J2) (Blasi et al., 1990) and has been used by numerous investigators as an effective alternative model system for primary microglia cultures to study various cell biology aspects (Henn et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Butyrate can stimulate a small but significant increase in MHC expression on BV2 cells.
source: Butyrate was able to stimulate a small, but significant, increase in MHC expression
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from BV2 cell stimulation experiments.

claim: The highest levels of MHCI and II upregulation on BV2 cells are achieved by bacterial-associated TLR ligands.
source: however, the highest levels of MHCI and II upregulation were achieved by bacterial-associated TLR ligands (Figure 5A,B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data from BV2 cell experiments in Figures 5A, 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: TLR ligands from the microbiota are able to prime microglia for antigen presentation.
source: These data suggest that TLR ligands from the microbiota are able to prime microglia for antigen presentation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the BV2 cell stimulation experiments showing TLR ligands upregulate MHC expression.

claim: There is no difference in the morphology of microglia from TLR deficient mice.
source: A previous report demonstrated that there is no difference in the morphology of microglia from TLR deficient mice (Erny et al., 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Gut microbial products are found circulating within the blood.
source: How TLR ligands signal to cells within the CNS is unclear, however, there is evidence that gut microbial products are found circulating within the blood and could reach the CNS through this route (Clarke et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: LPS is not able to penetrate the blood-brain barrier.
source: This requires further investigation as some reports have shown that LPS is not able to penetrate the blood–brain barrier.
evidence: The claim is stated as knowledge from previous reports, though not specifically cited.

claim: Enteroendocrine cells contain neuropods that are directly linked to neuronal cells and are able to transmit signals to the CNS.
source: Indeed, enteroendocrine cells have been reported to contain neuropods that are directly linked to neuronal cells and are able to transmit signals to the CNS (Bohórquez et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Cells from the gut can migrate to the brain.
source: Recent studies have demonstrated that cells from the gut can migrate to the brain and there exist a population of long-lived CX3CR1 cells within the gut (Shaw et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Gut-resident CX3CR1 cells are radio-sensitive while microglia are not.
source: As these gut cells are still radio-sensitive (microglia are not), our bone marrow chimera studies argue, that these cells likely only play a minor role, if any.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from bone marrow chimera experiments and known properties of microglia.

claim: There are several examples of cell wall molecules from the microbiota that are sufficient to treat disease in various animal models.
source: Indeed, there are several examples of cell wall molecules from the microbiota that are sufficient to treat disease in various animal models (An et al., 2014; Mazmanian et al., 2008; Vatanen et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: LPS from Bacteroides is less stimulatory than LPS derived from E. coli.
source: There are several different types of LPS that are derived from the microbiota, indeed LPS from Bacteriodes is less stimulatory than LPS derived from E. coli (Vatanen et al., 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Fatty acids produced by the microbiota are capable of binding TLR4.
source: Additionally, fatty acids that can be produced by the microbiota are also capable of binding TLR4, and might constitute other relevant agonists (Wong et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Microglia influence the function of neurons.
source: As microglia are also known to influence the function of neurons, these results suggest that microbial control of microglia could influence neuronal activity and function (Parkhurst et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature and inference from the current findings.

claim: Appropriate microbial stimulation is critical to steady state development of the CNS and optimum neurologic health.
source: Much remains to be explored regarding the mechanisms by which gut microbes influence the brain; however, our findings highlight that appropriate microbial stimulation is critical to steady state development of the CNS and optimum neurologic health.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the collective findings of the manuscript.

claim: Studies performed almost 50 years ago suggested that resident commensals aid in protection from influenza virus.
source: Consistent with the known contribution of the microbiota to immune system development, studies performed almost 50 years ago suggested that resident commensals aid in protection from influenza virus (Dolowy and Muldoon, 1964).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Many human neurotropic viral pathogens are associated with the development of neurologic dysfunction.
source: Many human neurotropic viral pathogens are associated with the development of neurologic dysfunction (Koyuncu et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Loss of immune stimulation by the gut microbiota leads to failure to control viral replication within the CNS leading to enhanced neuropathy.
source: Supporting this hypothesis, our findings demonstrate that loss of immune stimulation by the gut microbiota leads to failure to control viral replication within the CNS leading to enhanced neuropathy.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings in the manuscript.

claim: The microbiota influences serotonin production.
source: The microbiota influences serotonin production, microglia gene expression patterns, and disease pathology in a mouse model of Parkinson's disease (Erny et al., 2015; Reigstad et al., 2015; Sampson et al., 2016; Yano et al., 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The microbiota influences disease pathology in a mouse model of Parkinson's disease.
source: The microbiota influences serotonin production, microglia gene expression patterns, and disease pathology in a mouse model of Parkinson's disease (Erny et al., 2015; Reigstad et al., 2015; Sampson et al., 2016; Yano et al., 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Microglia develop early in embryogenesis from yolk sac progenitors.
source: Microglia develop early in embryogenesis from yolk sac progenitors; however, in contrast to macrophages, microglia are long-lived without any significant input from circulating blood cells (Prinz et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Microglia are long-lived without any significant input from circulating blood cells.
source: Microglia develop early in embryogenesis from yolk sac progenitors; however, in contrast to macrophages, microglia are long-lived without any significant input from circulating blood cells (Prinz et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Products from the microbiota are sufficient to prime microglia within the CNS that aid in control of viral replication through microglia-intrinsic TLR4 signaling.
source: We demonstrate that products from the microbiota are sufficient to prime microglia within the CNS that aid in control of viral replication through microglia-intrinsic TLR4 signaling.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the main findings of the manuscript.

claim: Reductions in microbial stimulation through increased antibiotic use and sanitation has been suggested to contribute to the significant increase in obesity, autoimmunity and some neurologic disorders in the western world.
source: Reductions in microbial stimulation through increased antibiotic use and sanitation, has been suggested to contribute to the significant increase in obesity, autoimmunity and even some neurologic disorders in the western world (Blaser, 2016; Strachan, 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Loss of protective resident microbes can lead to CNS dysfunction.
source: Thus, loss of protective resident microbes can lead to CNS dysfunction.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the findings of the manuscript.

claim: Viral infection of the CNS can cause permanent neurologic damage and psychiatric disorders.
source: Viral infection of the CNS can cause permanent neurologic damage and psychiatric disorders (Bergmann et al., 2006; Koyuncu et al., 2013; van den Pol, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Multiple viruses including Zika and West Nile virus have been associated with Guillain-Barre syndrome and memory deficits.
source: Indeed, multiple viruses including Zika and West Nile virus have been associated with Guillain-Barre syndrome and memory deficits, respectively (Carson et al., 2006; Parra et al., 2016; Vasek et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: CNS viral infection has been implicated in the initiation of Parkinson's disease, multiple sclerosis, Alzheimer's disease, narcolepsy and other chronic neurologic diseases.
source: Moreover, while Parkinson's disease, multiple sclerosis, Alzheimer's disease, narcolepsy and other chronic neurologic diseases have unknown etiologies, initiation by CNS viral infection has been implicated (Itzhaki et al., 2016; Kakalacheva et al., 2011; Stoessl, 1999; Tesoriero et al., 2016; Virtanen and Jacobson, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Resident cells of the CNS are often targets for viral infection and are critical in induction of distinct pro-inflammatory signatures that function to attract virus-specific lymphocytes into the CNS.
source: Resident cells of the CNS are often targets for infection and are critical in induction of distinct pro-inflammatory signatures that function to attract virus-specific lymphocytes into the CNS.
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge about CNS viral infections.

claim: A significant hurdle encountered by infiltrating antigen-specific lymphocytes is to eliminate virus from infected cells while limiting damage that may have long-term detrimental consequences to the host.
source: Consequently, a significant hurdle encountered by infiltrating antigen-specific lymphocytes is to eliminate virus from infected cells while limiting damage that may have long-term detrimental consequences to the host.
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge about CNS viral infections.

claim: The microbiota impacts both immune cell composition and functionality.
source: This is consistent with the known function of the microbiota on both immune cell composition and functionality (Belkaid and Hand, 2014; Hooper et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Commensal microbes promote CD4+ T helper cell responses both within and outside of the intestine.
source: In particular, commensal microbes promote CD4+ T helper cell responses both within and outside of the intestine (Atarashi et al., 2011; Ivanov et al., 2009; Lee et al., 2011; Mazmanian et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Germfree mice have slight systemic immune deficiencies in the response to intraperitoneal infection with MHV-DM in both total T cells and virus-specific T cells.
source: Consistent with published reports using other viruses, we observed slight systemic immune deficiencies in the response to i.p. infection with MHV-DM in GF mice in both total T cells and virus-specific T cells; only the number of viral-specific CD8+ T cells reached statistical significance (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–D) (Abt et al., 2012; Ichinohe et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-D and citations to previous literature.

claim: Treatment of West Nile Virus-infected mice with a CSF1R inhibitor results in limited viral control associated with impaired activation of antigen presenting cells in both blood and draining lymph nodes.
source: Recent studies have demonstrated that treatment of West Nile Virus-infected mice with a CSF1R inhibitor results in limited viral control associated with impaired activation of antigen presenting cells (APCs) in both blood and draining lymph nodes arguing that in addition to targeting microglia other immune cells are also depleted leading to a potentially immunosuppressed state (Funk and Klein, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Antigen presentation in TLR deficient mice was not evaluated in previous studies on microglia morphology.
source: A previous report demonstrated that there is no difference in the morphology of microglia from TLR deficient mice (Erny et al., 2015), but antigen presentation in these mice was not evaluated in these studies.
evidence: The claim identifies a gap in previous literature.
